subject: physics
title: Conservation of momentum and collisions
key_idea: In a closed system the total momentum is the same before and after an interaction. This holds in every collision and explosion. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

sections.heading: The principle of conservation of momentum

blocks.text: This section states the principle and explains why it is true.

items.meaning: A group of objects with no resultant external force acting on it.
The total momentum of a closed system stays constant.

items: The total momentum of a closed system before an interaction equals the total momentum after it.
Momentum is a vector, so give each momentum a sign in one dimension.
It follows from Newton's laws. The two objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other (third law).
The forces act for the same time, so the impulses are equal and opposite.
One object gains the momentum that the other loses, so the total does not change.
Total momentum is conserved when no external force acts.
It follows from Newton's second and third laws.

sections.heading: Collisions and explosions in one dimension

blocks.text: Choose a positive direction, then add up the momentum before and after.

blocks.label: Conservation of momentum
where: u₁, u₂ = velocities before, in m/s
v₁, v₂ = velocities after, in m/s

items.text: Add the momenta before. A cart of 2.0 kg at +3.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.0 kg cart: total = 6.0 kg m/s.
Add the momenta after. If the carts stick, total = (2.0 + 1.0) × v.
Set before equal to after: 6.0 = 3.0v, so v = 2.0 m/s.

diagram.alt: A slider for two trolleys that collide and stick together. It shows the shared velocity after the collision and the kinetic energy lost.

items: In an **explosion** the objects start together with zero total momentum.
They move apart with equal and opposite momenta, so the total is still zero.
The lighter piece moves away faster than the heavier piece.
Total momentum before = total momentum after, with signs for direction.
In an explosion from rest, the pieces have equal and opposite momenta.

blocks.text: Momentum is a vector, so it is conserved separately in each of two perpendicular directions.

items.text: Choose two perpendicular directions, for example x and y.
Split every velocity into components. A speed v at angle θ to the x-axis has components v cos θ and v sin θ.
Total x-momentum before = total x-momentum after.
Total y-momentum before = total y-momentum after.
Use Pythagoras and tan θ to find the final speed and direction.

items: If the total momentum is along x, the final y-components must cancel.
So the two objects leave on opposite sides of the x-axis, unless both stay on it.
Resolve into perpendicular components.
Momentum is conserved in each direction separately.

blocks.text: Momentum is always conserved. Kinetic energy may or may not be.

rows: Some is transferred to other forms, such as heat and sound
Relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation
Relative speed of separation is smaller than the relative speed of approach

items: To decide whether a collision is elastic, compare the total kinetic energy before and after.
If the totals are equal, it is elastic. If the total after is smaller, it is inelastic.
A **perfectly inelastic** collision is one where the objects stick together.
Kinetic energy cannot increase in a collision. In an explosion it does increase, because stored energy is released.
Momentum is conserved in all collisions.
Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.

checks.q: A 1500 kg car moving at 4.0 m/s hits a stationary 1000 kg car. They lock together. Calculate their speed immediately after the collision.
checks.a: Momentum before = 1500 × 4.0 = 6000 kg m/s. Momentum after = (1500 + 1000) × v. So v = 6000 / 2500 = 2.4 m/s.

checks.q: A stationary 0.50 kg trolley is released by a spring and moves off at 1.2 m/s. A 1.5 kg trolley moves the other way. Calculate its speed.
checks.a: Total momentum is zero, so the momenta are equal and opposite. 0.50 × 1.2 = 1.5 × v. So v = 0.40 m/s.

checks.q: Describe how you would decide whether a collision between two objects was elastic or inelastic.
checks.a: Calculate the total kinetic energy before and after the collision. If it is the same, the collision is elastic. If the total is less after, it is inelastic.

blocks.text: You must derive and use the kinetic energy of a non-relativistic particle in terms of its momentum.

items.text: Multiply the top and bottom by m: Eₖ = ½m²v² / m.

blocks.label: Kinetic energy in terms of momentum

items: For two particles with the same momentum, the lighter one has the **greater** kinetic energy.
Use this form when the momentum is known and the speed is not.
You must be able to **state** the principle of conservation of momentum.
For an elastic collision, recall that total kinetic energy is conserved. The relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation.
Problems can be elastic or inelastic, in one or two dimensions.
The coefficient of restitution is not needed.
Be able to apply the principle to collisions and other interactions of bodies, in one and in two dimensions.
Know the terms **perfectly elastic collision** and **inelastic collision**.
